summary: A 46-second creator reel that names a 'Taste Index': point an AI at one website you love, have it break down that site's fonts, colors, shapes, components, motion and voice, and turn them into a reusable guide the AI reads before building anything new. The on-screen prompt asks for four files (a DESIGN.md with a one-line brief, 5-7 principles and a Do / Don't list that explains why, a CSS file of variables, a motion script and a live specimen page), and asks the agent to mark what it measured versus made up. Two example cards show the same five-line format (Brief, Color, Shape, Motion, Never) holding two opposite tastes. For a design system this matters as a format: a short, plain taste summary that any agent can hold in its head. It conflicts with OpenDesigner on one point: the example copies one brand's identity wholesale.
key_ideas: Generic AI output comes from the AI having no written reference for what good looks like.
A written visual reference, read before every build, keeps new pages in one visual language.
The guide should explain why each rule exists, so the agent can handle cases the guide did not cover.
One fixed format can hold opposite tastes: Brief, Color, Shape, Motion, Never.
A one-line brief written as a concrete picture says more than adjectives.
Motion can be written as a feeling plus a test, not only as durations.
The agent should say which values it measured and which it invented.
A live specimen page that shows every swatch, size and component is part of the guide.
Extracting from a single site also copies that site's identity [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: The source recommends a Taste Index built from a site you love, kept as files the AI reads before every build.
decisions.evidence: I started using something I call a Taste Index to give Claude a reference

process.detail: Open a few different pages, not only the home page, and read the computed styles: fonts, every color and where it is used, borders, radius, shadows, spacing and grid, repeating components, motion and easing, and how headlines, labels and buttons are written.

DESIGN.md (a one-line brief, 5-7 principles, then color, type, components, motion and a Do / Don't list, with reasons), a CSS file with every value as a variable plus component classes, a motion script with no dependencies, and a live page showing every swatch, size and component.
Attach an existing Taste Index as the example and match its structure and depth, not its look.
Mark measured versus made-up values, open the live page, list what was uncertain, and add one line to CLAUDE.md so later agents read the guide first.

caveats: Self-promotion, left out of the rules: 'comment TASTE' to receive the prompt, and a follow request (0:38 to the end, and the caption).

Most rules, numbers and examples were read from frames (the on-screen prompt and pages, 0:22 to 0:41), not spoken; the raw file's on-screen section was transcribed from full-resolution frames on 2026-10-15.

The example index copies typesafe.ai's identity (its colors and look) for the presenter's own content. OpenDesigner's identity rule forbids that: references give structure and quality, never a brand's identity. Use the format, not the copying. [inferred conflict with SPEC 5.4]
The 90/9/1 ratio is one person's taste card, not evidence; OpenDesigner's research keeps accent use as a soft guide (about 15% of a view, DC-L15-03) and treats 60-30-10 as weak evidence.
Auto-captions: 'the Jev website' refers to typesafe.ai (TypeSafe's model is named Jev, shown in the frames); 'your CTO' may be a mis-hearing of the presenter's name or handle.
Product tag judged here: the source shows only marketing and resource pages, but the technique is not specific to either, so rules are tagged both. [inferred]
